one_liner: Schema-compiled binary serializer for C++ and eight other languages; about 4x lower serialize/deserialize latency than Protobuf on small messages.
what_it_does: You write enums, flags and structs in a .fbe schema. The fbec compiler turns it into C++ domain structs plus Model/FinalModel classes (and matching C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Kotlin, Python, Ruby and Swift code) that all read and write one binary format. In C++ the sender calls `AccountModel::serialize(obj)` and ships `buffer()`; the receiver calls `attach()`, optionally `verify()`, then `deserialize(obj)`. Extra generator flags add JSON conversion (RapidJSON) and Sender/Receiver/Client protocol classes. It is not wire- or API-compatible with protobuf, so switching means rewriting both the schema and the call sites.
how_it_is_fast: Every struct field has a fixed size and a fixed offset set in the generated code. Fields are read and written as little-endian values through direct pointer-cast loads and stores, with no varint/zigzag coding and no per-field tag parsing. Strings, vectors, optionals and nested structs live out of line behind 4-byte offsets, and their space comes from appending to one growable malloc buffer that is reused after `reset()`. Versioning uses a size-and-type header on each struct, so old readers skip unknown trailing fields without parsing tags. The optional `--final` model drops those headers and offsets to get smaller, faster output, at the cost of versioning.
when_to_use: Small structured messages of a few hundred bytes (orders, account updates, RPC requests) where per-message encode/decode latency matters more than wire size.
C++ services that exchange the same messages with C#, Go, Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, JavaScript or Swift peers and want one schema that generates code for all of them.
Protocols that need to evolve: you can append fields, enum values and flags, and old and new readers/writers still interoperate. Struct inheritance lets you extend a third-party schema.
Frozen protocols that can use `--final`: FBE's own (older) README table shows 152 vs 252 bytes and 57/81 vs 88/98 ns serialize/deserialize for the final model versus the versioned one.
Projects that want generated Sender/Receiver/Client classes and JSON conversion from the same schema instead of combining separate libraries.
when_not_to_use: When message size matters most: on the benchmark message FBE produces 234 bytes versus 120 for Protobuf, because it uses fixed-width fields and 4-byte offsets instead of varints (the final model gets this down to 152 bytes).
C++-only code with no cross-language need: on the same benchmark page SimpleBinaryEncoding (35/52 ns) and zpp::bits (34/37 ns) are about 2x faster, and zpp::bits needs no IDL.
Read-mostly zero-copy access: FlatBuffers deserializes in 81 ns versus FBE's 84 ns, and FBE's `deserialize()` copies into std::string/std::vector domain objects.

Embedded or unusual targets: the generated fbe.cpp throws exceptions, so -fno-exceptions builds fail (issue #76, open). Platform code covers only Unix and Windows. The fbec build fails on Windows ARM64 and Win32 (issue #108). The C++ generator contains no byte-swapping code, so big-endian hosts are unsupported.
When you rely on the protobuf ecosystem (gRPC, many third-party tools, oneof/variants): FBE has no union/variant type (issue #55, open) and no vcpkg package (issue #65, open).

integration.dependencies: Generated C++ needs libuuid on Linux/macOS or Rpcrt4 on Windows. {fmt} >= 9 is optional (formatting) and RapidJSON is needed only for --json output. Building the fbec compiler needs CMake 3.20+, flex, bison, python3 with the gil tool, CppCommon and cpp-optparse.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 for the generated code (std::optional, per the README). The repo's own build sets C++23 through CppCMakeScripts and needs CMake 3.20.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows; CI covers GCC, Clang, MSVC, MinGW, MSYS2 and Cygwin. Assumes a little-endian host. The fbec build fails on Windows ARM64/Win32 (issue #108).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Models are not safe to share: even the const `deserialize()` shifts the shared buffer offset, so give each thread its own model. The generated request/response Client uses a std::mutex internally.

gotchas: The README's C++ examples show a stale template API (`AccountModel<FBE::WriteBuffer>`). Code generated by 1.15.0.0 has a non-template `AccountModel` over `FBEBuffer`, so follow examples/ or CppSerialization instead.

`deserialize()` does not validate the whole message. A field that fails its bounds check silently becomes its default in release builds, and asserts fire only in debug builds. Call `verify()` on untrusted input; the timed FBE deserialize loop in the benchmark leaves it out.

`FBEBuffer::allocate()`/`reserve()` have no size limit and do not check whether malloc() failed (issue #107, open). `FBEBuffer::remove()` uses memcpy on ranges that can overlap. All offsets are uint32, which caps a message at 4 GiB.
Linux builds fail to link unless you add libuuid (issue #89: undefined `uuid_generate_time`). The fbec build pulls in flex/bison and the author's gil-managed submodules.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FBE over Cista++, struct_pack, YAS or bitsery when the same messages must also be read from C#, Go, Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, JavaScript or Swift, or when you want schema versioning plus a generated sender/receiver protocol. For C++-only code those siblings serialize plain structs with no IDL or codegen step.
verified_claims_summary: The author's CppSerialization page (CppBenchmark; Apple M1 Pro; 'release' configuration, with compiler and flags not stated; run 2025-07-16) times one Account with a wallet and three orders. FBE takes 77 ns to serialize and 84 ns to deserialize; Protobuf takes 322/351 ns, about 4.2x slower. In that setup Protobuf builds a fresh message per operation with no arena, and FBE's verify() runs outside the timed loop. The 66/82 vs 628/759 ns table still in FBE's README comes from a stale 2018 Intel/Windows run.
status_note: Single-maintainer and sporadically maintained: the last functional release was 1.15.0.0 (2025-07-16, compile fixes), the newest commit (2026-09-10) only renamed the default branch, and 36 issues are open. It is MIT-licensed, and the generated C++ is plain source you vendor into your tree.
